concepts.def: A globular protein that acts as a biological catalyst, increasing the rate of one specific chemical reaction by lowering its activation energy. The enzyme is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction, so a single enzyme molecule can catalyse the same reaction many times over.

A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or permanently altered. The reaction could occur without the catalyst, but at the temperatures found in cells most metabolic reactions would be far too slow to sustain life, so cells depend on enzymes to bring rates up to a useful level.

The complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions occurring in a living organism. Almost every reaction is catalysed by its own specific enzyme, so an organism needs many different enzymes, and it can exert control over metabolism by controlling the amount and activity of those enzymes.

A sequence of enzyme-catalysed reactions in which the product of one reaction is the substrate of the next, arranged either as a linear chain or as a cycle. Pathways link with one another to form the network of metabolism.

Regulation of the rate of a metabolic pathway by regulating its enzymes: how much of each enzyme is synthesized and whether each enzyme molecule is active. This is possible only because each reaction depends on a specific enzyme, so inhibiting or activating one enzyme adjusts one pathway without affecting the rest of metabolism.

The metabolic reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones, including the formation of macromolecules from monomers by condensation reactions. Protein synthesis, glycogen formation and photosynthesis are anabolic. Anabolic reactions require an input of energy, usually from ATP.

The metabolic reactions that break larger molecules into smaller ones, including the hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers during digestion and the oxidation of substrates such as glucose in cell respiration. Catabolic reactions release energy.

A reaction in which two molecules are joined by a covalent bond and a water molecule is released. Monomers are linked into macromolecules by condensation: amino acids into polypeptides by peptide bonds, and glucose into glycogen by glycosidic bonds.

A reaction in which a covalent bond within a molecule is broken by the addition of a water molecule. Macromolecules are digested into monomers by hydrolysis, for example starch into maltose and then glucose, and polypeptides into amino acids.

A protein folded into a compact, roughly spherical three-dimensional shape that is held by interactions between amino acids, including hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions. Enzymes are globular proteins, and it is this folding that creates the active site.

The region of an enzyme to which the substrate binds and where catalysis occurs. It is composed of only a few amino acids, but interactions between amino acids throughout the folded three-dimensional structure of the enzyme hold those few amino acids in the positions that give the active site the shape and chemical properties needed for catalysis.

The model of enzyme-substrate binding in which the active site is not a rigid shape that exactly matches the substrate. As the substrate binds, interactions between it and the active site cause both the enzyme and the substrate to change shape, giving a closer fit and weakening bonds within the substrate so that the reaction is catalysed.

The temporary structure formed while a substrate is bound to the active site of an enzyme. Within the complex the substrate is converted to product, which is then released, leaving the active site free to bind another substrate molecule.

The random encounter of a substrate molecule with the active site of an enzyme, which must happen before binding can occur. Both substrate and enzyme move by random molecular motion in the fluid around them, and the rate of reaction depends on how often collisions occur with the substrate in an orientation that allows binding.

An enzyme held in a fixed position, for example by being embedded in a membrane. Catalysis still occurs because substrate molecules move randomly and collide with the active site. Conversely, some very large substrate molecules are effectively immobile, and it is the enzyme that moves to them.

The property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or one type of reaction. It arises because the shape and the chemical properties (charge and polarity) of the active site are complementary to one substrate, so other molecules do not bind in a way that allows catalysis.

A change in the three-dimensional structure of a protein caused, for example, by high temperature or extreme pH, which breaks the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions that hold the folded shape; the peptide bonds remain intact. In an enzyme the active site loses its complementary shape, so the substrate can no longer bind and activity is lost, usually permanently.

Reaction occurs when a substrate and an active site collide with sufficient energy and in the correct orientation. Factors that increase the frequency or energy of collisions, such as higher temperature or higher substrate concentration, increase the rate until some other factor, such as denaturation or saturation of active sites, limits it.

The temperature at which an enzyme's rate of activity is highest. Below it, rate rises with temperature because molecules move faster and so collide more often and with more energy. Above it, rate falls steeply because the enzyme is denatured.

The pH at which an enzyme's rate of activity is highest; it differs between enzymes (about 2 for pepsin in the stomach, about 8 for trypsin in the small intestine). Away from the optimum, changes in hydrogen ion concentration alter the charges on amino acids, disrupting ionic and hydrogen bonds and changing the shape of the active site; at extreme pH the enzyme is denatured.

The state reached at high substrate concentration when every active site is occupied almost all of the time. Rate rises with substrate concentration because collisions with active sites become more frequent, but the rise slows and the rate reaches a plateau at saturation, when adding more substrate cannot increase it further.

A generalized sketch of the relationship between a variable such as temperature and the rate of enzyme activity is a model: a simplified representation of a general pattern, not a record of the data from one experiment. Like other models in biology it can be evaluated using results from enzyme experiments and refined if the data disagree with it.

The change in the amount (mass, volume or concentration) of product formed or substrate used per unit time, for example cm³ of oxygen per second. It is found from the gradient of a graph of product or substrate against time, or as 1 divided by the time taken for a fixed change to occur.

The rate measured at the very start of a reaction, when the substrate concentration is known and has not yet fallen and no product has accumulated. It is found from the gradient of the first, steepest part of the graph and is the most reliable measure for comparing different conditions.

The energy that must be supplied to substrate molecules before a reaction can proceed, because energy is required to break bonds within the substrate. Enzymes lower the activation energy by binding the substrate in a way that strains and weakens these bonds, so that at cell temperatures far more substrate molecules have enough energy to react.

The net energy released when the bonds that form the products are made, after the energy needed to break the bonds in the substrate has been supplied. On an energy graph it is the difference between the energy level of the substrate and that of the products, and it is not changed by the presence of an enzyme.
An enzyme that acts inside the cell that synthesized it. The enzymes of glycolysis, which act in the cytoplasm, and of the Krebs cycle, which act in the mitochondrial matrix, are intracellular.

An enzyme that is synthesized inside a cell and secreted to act outside cells. The digestive enzymes of the gut, such as amylase, pepsin and lipase, are extracellular: they carry out chemical digestion by hydrolysing macromolecules in the gut lumen.

Heat released by the reactions of metabolism. Energy transfers in metabolic reactions are not 100% efficient, so some energy is converted to heat in every reaction; heat generation is therefore inevitable in every living cell. Mammals, birds and some other animals depend on this heat production to maintain a constant body temperature.

A metabolic pathway in which a chain of enzyme-catalysed reactions converts a starting substrate through a series of intermediates into a final product, with no intermediate regenerated. Glycolysis, which converts glucose to pyruvate, is a linear pathway.

A metabolic pathway in which the product of the final reaction is the substrate of the first, so that one intermediate is regenerated with every turn; other substrates enter the cycle and net products leave it. The Krebs cycle, which regenerates oxaloacetate, and the Calvin cycle, which regenerates RuBP, are cyclical pathways.

A binding site on an enzyme away from the active site, to which only specific substances can bind. Binding causes interactions within the enzyme that lead to conformational changes, altering the active site enough to prevent catalysis. Binding is reversible, so activity returns when the substance leaves the site.

Inhibition in which an inhibitor binds reversibly to an allosteric site rather than to the active site, changing the conformation of the enzyme so that the active site no longer catalyses the reaction. Because the inhibitor does not compete with the substrate, increasing the substrate concentration does not overcome the inhibition and the maximum rate is lowered.

Inhibition by a substance that resembles the substrate and binds reversibly to the active site, so that substrate and inhibitor compete for the same site. Increasing the substrate concentration reduces the effect of the inhibitor, and at a high enough substrate concentration the rate approaches the uninhibited maximum.

Drugs used to lower blood cholesterol. They are competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme in the pathway that synthesizes cholesterol: a statin resembles the enzyme's substrate and binds reversibly to the active site, reducing the rate of cholesterol synthesis in liver cells.

Regulation of a metabolic pathway in which the end product acts as an inhibitor, usually by binding to an allosteric site on the first enzyme of the pathway. When the end product accumulates the pathway slows; as the end product is used up, inhibition is released. In the pathway that converts threonine to isoleucine, isoleucine inhibits the first enzyme, threonine deaminase.

Irreversible inhibition in which the inhibitor binds to the active site and the enzyme's own catalytic action converts it into a form that bonds covalently to the active site. The chemical change to the active site leaves the enzyme permanently inactive. Penicillin is an example.

A bacterial enzyme that forms cross-links between peptidoglycan strands in the cell wall. Penicillin binds irreversibly to its active site, so cross-linking fails, the wall is weakened and the cell bursts. In resistant bacteria a changed transpeptidase has an altered active site that still cross-links peptidoglycan but no longer binds penicillin effectively.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?
options: It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.
It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.
mcqs.specStatementText: Enzymes speed up reactions without being used up
mcqs.explain: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and the enzyme is not consumed, so each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.
rationales: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and the enzyme is not consumed, so each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.
A student who treats the enzyme as a reactant picks this. In fact the enzyme is released unchanged when the product leaves the active site; it is not consumed.

A student who has only ever seen the catalysed reaction picks this. In fact the reaction can occur without the enzyme; the enzyme increases its rate, which at cell temperature is otherwise far too slow to sustain life.
A student who thinks enzymes 'help' by supplying energy picks this. In fact the enzyme lowers the activation energy; the energy for reaction comes from the substrate molecules' own kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: Catalase in liver cells increases the rate at which hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen by a factor of many millions. What is the benefit to the cell of this increase in rate?
options: Hydrogen peroxide could not be broken down at all without an enzyme to make it possible.
Toxic hydrogen peroxide is removed fast enough at cell temperature to prevent damage.
Catalase supplies the energy that the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide needs.
The reaction releases energy that the cell captures as ATP, as in respiration.
mcqs.specStatementText: Enzymes speed up reactions without being used up
mcqs.explain: The benefit of increasing rates of reaction in cells is that reactions which would be uselessly slow at cell temperature happen fast enough to be useful. Here a toxic substance is destroyed before it can harm the cell.
rationales: A student who thinks enzymes make reactions possible rather than faster picks this. In fact hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly on its own; catalase increases the rate enormously.

The benefit of increasing rates of reaction in cells is that reactions which would be uselessly slow at cell temperature happen fast enough to be useful. Here a toxic substance is destroyed before it can harm the cell.
A student who thinks enzymes provide energy picks this. In fact catalase lowers the activation energy; it does not supply energy to the substrate.

A student who thinks every metabolic reaction is an energy-yielding reaction like respiration picks this. In fact the cell does not harvest energy from this reaction; its purpose is to remove a toxic product.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes metabolism in a living organism?
options: The set of reactions that release energy from food molecules to keep the organism alive and active.
A series of reactions whose rate is set only by how much substrate the organism takes in from outside.
A network of interdependent enzyme-catalysed reactions, each controlled through its own enzyme.
A set of reactions catalysed by a few general-purpose enzymes that act on many substrates.
mcqs.specStatementText: Metabolism is a network of reactions, each with its own enzyme
mcqs.explain: Metabolism is the complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions in an organism. Because each reaction depends on a specific enzyme, control over metabolism can be exerted through these enzymes.
rationales: A student who uses the everyday meaning of metabolism picks this. In fact metabolism includes anabolic reactions such as protein synthesis and photosynthesis as well as energy-releasing catabolic ones.
A student who thinks enzymes cannot be regulated picks this. In fact cells control metabolism by controlling the synthesis and activity of specific enzymes, not just by the supply of substrate.

Metabolism is the complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions in an organism. Because each reaction depends on a specific enzyme, control over metabolism can be exerted through these enzymes.
A student who thinks enzymes are all-purpose catalysts picks this. In fact enzyme specificity means each reaction needs its own enzyme, which is why organisms require many different enzymes.

mcqs.q: A yeast cell synthesizes one amino acid through a pathway of several steps. Why does this pathway require several different enzymes rather than one?
options: One enzyme could catalyse every step if the substrates were supplied in the correct order.
Each step needs a different amount of energy, and each enzyme supplies a fixed amount of energy.
Enzymes are used up as they work, so several are needed to complete all the steps.
Each step has a different substrate, and an active site fits only one substrate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Metabolism is a network of reactions, each with its own enzyme
mcqs.explain: Because of enzyme specificity, each enzyme's active site is complementary to one substrate, so each reaction in the pathway needs its own enzyme. This is why living organisms require many different enzymes.
rationales: A student who thinks an enzyme is a general-purpose catalyst picks this. In fact one active site cannot be complementary to several different substrates, so several enzymes are needed.
A student who thinks enzymes supply energy picks this. In fact enzymes lower activation energy and supply no energy; the number of enzymes is set by specificity, not by energy demands.
A student who thinks enzymes are consumed picks this. In fact each enzyme is released unchanged after every reaction, so a single enzyme molecule could serve its step indefinitely.

Because of enzyme specificity, each enzyme's active site is complementary to one substrate, so each reaction in the pathway needs its own enzyme. This is why living organisms require many different enzymes.

mcqs.q: Which process is an example of anabolism?
options: The formation of glycogen from glucose monomers by condensation reactions
The oxidation of glucose in cell respiration to provide ATP for the cell
The digestion of starch in the gut into maltose and then glucose
The hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, which releases energy
mcqs.specStatementText: Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
mcqs.explain: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones; the formation of macromolecules such as glycogen from monomers by condensation is one of the guide's named examples, along with protein synthesis and photosynthesis.
rationales: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones; the formation of macromolecules such as glycogen from monomers by condensation is one of the guide's named examples, along with protein synthesis and photosynthesis.

A student who classifies respiration as anabolic because it makes ATP picks this. In fact respiration oxidizes glucose to smaller molecules, so it is catabolic; ATP is the energy carrier, not a macromolecule being built.
A student who thinks digestion is anabolic because it produces useful monomers picks this. In fact digestion is hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers, a catabolic process.
A student who thinks anabolic reactions are the ones that release energy picks this. In fact anabolic reactions require energy; hydrolysis of ATP is a breaking-down reaction that releases it.

mcqs.q: In the small intestine, maltase converts each maltose molecule into two glucose molecules. How is this reaction classified?
options: Anabolic; the glucose produced is a useful new molecule that the body can then absorb and make use of
Catabolic; a hydrolysis reaction in which a water molecule is used to break the glycosidic bond
Catabolic; a condensation reaction in which a water molecule is released as the bond is broken
Catabolic; energy from ATP is needed to force the two glucose units of the maltose apart
mcqs.specStatementText: Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
mcqs.explain: Digestion of a larger molecule into monomers is catabolism, and the bond between the two glucose units is broken by the addition of water, which is hydrolysis.
rationales: A student who judges by whether the product is useful picks this. In fact the classification depends on the substrate being broken into smaller molecules, which makes it catabolic.
Digestion of a larger molecule into monomers is catabolism, and the bond between the two glucose units is broken by the addition of water, which is hydrolysis.
A student who attaches water release to bond breaking picks this. In fact condensation joins monomers and releases water; breaking the bond uses water and is hydrolysis.
A student who thinks breaking molecules down needs an input of energy picks this. In fact hydrolysis in digestion releases energy overall and does not consume ATP.

mcqs.q: A mutation replaces one amino acid in an enzyme at a position on the surface far from the active site in the folded protein. The enzyme loses most of its activity. What is the best explanation?
options: The result must be an error, because only the amino acids of the active site itself can affect catalysis
The loss of activity shows the enzyme has been denatured, so its chain has broken up into free amino acids
The change disturbs interactions that hold the enzyme's overall shape, altering the active site
The changed amino acid supplies less energy to the reaction, so the substrate cannot react
mcqs.specStatementText: The active site is a few amino acids held in place by the whole fold
mcqs.explain: The active site is composed of a few amino acids only, but interactions between amino acids within the overall three-dimensional structure ensure that it has the properties needed for catalysis. A change elsewhere can shift those interactions and distort the active site.
rationales: A student who thinks the rest of the enzyme is inert packaging picks this. In fact the whole three-dimensional structure positions and shapes the active site.

A student who equates any loss of enzyme activity with the polypeptide breaking up picks this. In fact a substitution leaves every peptide bond intact; the chain is complete but folds slightly differently, which is enough to alter the active site.

The active site is composed of a few amino acids only, but interactions between amino acids within the overall three-dimensional structure ensure that it has the properties needed for catalysis. A change elsewhere can shift those interactions and distort the active site.
A student who thinks enzymes supply energy to substrates picks this. In fact enzymes supply no energy; activity is lost because the active site's shape or chemistry has changed.

mcqs.q: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?
options: The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.
The enzyme seizes the substrate and holds it without any changes.
Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.
mcqs.specStatementText: Enzyme and substrate both change shape as they bind
mcqs.explain: Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.
rationales: A student still using the lock-and-key model picks this. In fact the active site is not rigid: it changes shape as the substrate binds.
A student who has noticed only the enzyme's movement picks this. In fact the substrate also changes shape on binding, and that change weakens its bonds.
A student who imagines enzymes actively catching substrates picks this. In fact substrate and active site meet by random collision, and both change shape once bound.
Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.

mcqs.q: ATP synthase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and cannot move freely. How do its substrates, ADP and phosphate, reach its active site?
options: They move by random molecular motion in the fluid and collide with the fixed active site.
They cannot, so an enzyme fixed in a membrane works only after being released from it.
The enzyme extends its active site out into the fluid to capture passing substrates.
They are carried to the enzyme by a directed flow of fluid in the mitochondrion.
mcqs.specStatementText: Random motion brings substrate and active site together
mcqs.explain: Movement is needed for a substrate and an active site to come together, but movement of the substrate alone is enough. Enzymes immobilized in membranes are reached by substrates moving randomly.
rationales: Movement is needed for a substrate and an active site to come together, but movement of the substrate alone is enough. Enzymes immobilized in membranes are reached by substrates moving randomly.
A student who thinks both partners must move picks this. In fact substrate molecules moving randomly collide with the active site of an immobilized enzyme, which works normally.
A student who imagines enzymes reaching for substrates picks this. In fact enzymes do not seek substrates; collisions arise from random molecular motion.
A student who thinks molecules stay still unless carried picks this. In fact molecules in a fluid are in constant random motion, which alone brings them into collision with the active site.

mcqs.q: Lipase catalyses the hydrolysis of triglycerides but has no effect on starch. What is the reason?
options: Starch molecules are too large to enter the active site, but any molecule smaller than starch could.
The active site of lipase is complementary in shape and chemical properties to a triglyceride only.
Starch requires more energy to break down than lipase is able to supply to the reaction.
Lipase seeks out triglyceride molecules in the fluid and ignores starch molecules it meets.
mcqs.specStatementText: Active site shape explains specificity and why denaturation stops activity
mcqs.explain: Enzyme-substrate specificity arises from the structure of the active site: its shape and chemical properties match one substrate, so starch cannot bind in a way that allows catalysis.
rationales: A student who thinks specificity is only a matter of size picks this. In fact many molecules smaller than starch also fail to bind, because the active site must match shape and chemistry.
Enzyme-substrate specificity arises from the structure of the active site: its shape and chemical properties match one substrate, so starch cannot bind in a way that allows catalysis.
A student who thinks enzymes supply energy picks this. In fact enzymes supply no energy; lipase fails to act on starch because starch does not fit its active site.
A student who imagines enzymes choosing their targets picks this. In fact lipase collides with all molecules at random; only a triglyceride binds productively to its active site.

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: Its peptide bonds are broken, so the polypeptide chain splits into its separate amino acids.
Its shape alters only briefly and then returns to normal once the conditions are restored.
Its three-dimensional structure changes, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.
It is killed, because enzymes are living particles that are destroyed by heat or acid.
mcqs.specStatementText: Active site shape explains specificity and why denaturation stops activity
mcqs.explain: Denaturation disrupts the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions that hold the enzyme's folded shape. The active site loses the shape and properties needed to bind the substrate, so activity is lost.
rationales: A student who thinks denaturation destroys the molecule picks this. In fact the peptide bonds and primary structure remain intact; only the folding changes.
A student who extends the reversibility of low temperature to denaturation picks this. In fact denaturation is usually permanent; the enzyme does not refold correctly.

Denaturation disrupts the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions that hold the enzyme's folded shape. The active site loses the shape and properties needed to bind the substrate, so activity is lost.
A student who takes 'killed' literally picks this. In fact enzymes are protein molecules, not living things; heat or extreme pH changes their shape.

mcqs.q: A student measured the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at six temperatures. The rates, in arbitrary units, were: 10 °C, 2; 20 °C, 4; 30 °C, 8; 40 °C, 15; 50 °C, 9; 60 °C, 1. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
options: The low rate at 10 °C shows that the enzyme had been denatured by the cold temperature.
The true optimum is 37 °C, the body temperature at which every enzyme works at its best.
The fall in rate after 40 °C shows that the substrate had been used up at higher temperatures.
The optimum is near 40 °C; above it, denaturation outweighs the faster collisions.
mcqs.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
mcqs.explain: Rate rises with temperature up to 40 °C as molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often and more energetically. Above the optimum, denaturation of the enzyme reduces the rate sharply.
rationales: A student who treats both ends of the graph the same way picks this. In fact the low rate in the cold is due to slower molecular motion and fewer collisions; the enzyme's structure is unchanged.
A student who assumes all enzymes share the human body's conditions picks this. In fact optima differ between enzymes, and these data show the highest rate at 40 °C.
A student who confuses a rate-temperature graph with a product-time graph picks this. In fact each rate was measured with fresh substrate; the fall is caused by denaturation.
Rate rises with temperature up to 40 °C as molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often and more energetically. Above the optimum, denaturation of the enzyme reduces the rate sharply.

mcqs.q: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?
options: Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.
The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
The amount of energy the enzyme can supply each second has reached its upper limit.
mcqs.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
mcqs.explain: At saturation the enzyme is working at its maximum rate: as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.
rationales: At saturation the enzyme is working at its maximum rate: as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.
A student who thinks enzymes are consumed picks this. In fact enzymes are released unchanged; the plateau reflects saturation of active sites, not loss of enzyme.
A student who assumes substrate has a damaging limit like temperature picks this. In fact substrate concentration does not change the enzyme's structure.
A student who thinks enzymes supply energy picks this. In fact enzymes supply no energy; the limit is the number of active sites available for substrate to bind.

mcqs.q: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. When it passes with food into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, its activity falls almost to zero. Which explanation is correct?
options: The alkaline conditions hydrolyse the peptide bonds of pepsin, breaking it up into free amino acids.
The change in pH alters charges on amino acids, disrupting bonds that hold the active site's shape.
Pepsin has run out of substrate, because protein digestion is completed inside the stomach.
At pH 8 the enzyme and substrate molecules move more slowly, so they collide less often.
mcqs.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
mcqs.explain: Hydrogen ion concentration affects the charges on amino acids in the enzyme. Away from the optimum, ionic and hydrogen bonds are disrupted, the active site changes shape and at an extreme the enzyme is denatured.
rationales: A student who thinks loss of activity means the chain is broken picks this. In fact the peptide bonds are intact; the enzyme's folded shape has been disrupted.

Hydrogen ion concentration affects the charges on amino acids in the enzyme. Away from the optimum, ionic and hydrogen bonds are disrupted, the active site changes shape and at an extreme the enzyme is denatured.
A student who looks for a substrate explanation picks this. In fact protein digestion is far from complete in the stomach; pepsin is inactive at pH 8 because its structure is altered.
A student who applies the temperature explanation to pH picks this. In fact pH does not change molecular speed; it acts on the enzyme's structure.

mcqs.q: A textbook sketch graph shows the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction rising steadily with temperature to a sharp peak and then falling steeply. A class measured catalase activity every 5 °C from 5 °C to 70 °C and found a broad plateau between 30 °C and 45 °C rather than a sharp peak. How should the sketch graph be regarded?
options: As an accurate record of catalase results, which shows that the class must have made an error somewhere.
As a model that the mismatch has proved to be wrong, so it should be discarded and not used again.
As a model of the general relationship, which the class data can be used to evaluate and refine.
As a graph of one specific enzyme that was measured, so it says nothing about catalase.
mcqs.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
mcqs.explain: Generalized sketches of relationships are models. The class results neither prove nor disprove the sketch outright; they are evidence for evaluating it, and here suggest that for catalase the peak should be drawn as a plateau.
rationales: A student who treats a sketch graph as data picks this. In fact a sketch has no data points or scale; it is a simplified model and cannot overrule real measurements.
A student who thinks a model is simply right or wrong picks this. In fact a mismatch leads to evaluation and refinement; the general pattern of rise, optimum and fall is still supported.

Generalized sketches of relationships are models. The class results neither prove nor disprove the sketch outright; they are evidence for evaluating it, and here suggest that for catalase the peak should be drawn as a plateau.
A student who thinks the sketch records one enzyme's results picks this. In fact it is a generalized model intended to apply to enzymes in general, which is exactly why catalase data can test it.

mcqs.q: Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 cm³; 20 s, 12 cm³; 40 s, 20 cm³; 60 s, 24 cm³. What is the initial rate of reaction?
options: 0.40 cm³ s⁻¹
1.7 s per cm³
20 cm³ in 40 s
0.6 cm³ s⁻¹
mcqs.specStatementText: Rate is change in product or substrate per unit time
mcqs.explain: The initial rate is the gradient of the first, steepest part of the graph: 12 cm³ of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 / 20 = 0.6 cm³ s⁻¹.
rationales: A student who divides the final volume by the whole time (24 / 60) picks this. That is a mean rate over a period in which the reaction had already slowed; the initial rate uses the first interval.
A student who divides time by volume (20 / 12) picks this. Rate is amount per unit time, so the volume is divided by the time, not the other way round.

A student who quotes a reading rather than a rate picks this. A rate must be expressed as a change per unit time, and 20 / 40 would in any case be a mean over a period when the rate had already fallen.
The initial rate is the gradient of the first, steepest part of the graph: 12 cm³ of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 / 20 = 0.6 cm³ s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: A filter-paper disc soaked in catalase solution sinks in hydrogen peroxide and rises when enough oxygen has formed on it. In 1% hydrogen peroxide the disc took 50 s to rise; in 2% it took 20 s. Which statement about the reaction rate is correct?
options: Rate is proportional to 1/time, so the rate at 2% (0.05 s⁻¹) is 2.5 times the rate at 1% (0.02 s⁻¹).
The rate at 1% is 50 and at 2% is 20, so the rate fell when the concentration was doubled.
Doubling the concentration doubles the rate, so the rate at 2% is 0.04 s⁻¹, twice that at 1%.
The rate cannot be found, because the volume of oxygen produced was not measured in either trial.
mcqs.specStatementText: Rate is change in product or substrate per unit time
mcqs.explain: A fixed event, the disc rising, takes less time when the reaction is faster, so rate is proportional to 1/time: 1/20 = 0.05 s⁻¹ and 1/50 = 0.02 s⁻¹, a ratio of 2.5.
rationales: A fixed event, the disc rising, takes less time when the reaction is faster, so rate is proportional to 1/time: 1/20 = 0.05 s⁻¹ and 1/50 = 0.02 s⁻¹, a ratio of 2.5.
A student who reports the measured time as the rate picks this. In fact a shorter time means a faster reaction; rates must be calculated as 1/time before they are compared.
A student who assumes rate is always proportional to substrate concentration picks this and calculates instead of using the data. The measured times give 0.05 s⁻¹, not 0.04 s⁻¹.
A student who thinks a rate must come from an amount of product picks this. In fact the time taken for a fixed change is a valid measure, with rate proportional to 1/time.

mcqs.q: How does an enzyme affect the energy changes of the reaction it catalyses?
options: It lowers the energy of the products, so that more energy is released overall than would be without the enzyme.
It lowers the activation energy but leaves the energy difference between substrate and products unchanged.
It supplies the activation energy, transferring its own energy to the substrate to break the bonds.
It releases energy by breaking bonds in the substrate, and this provides the activation energy.
mcqs.specStatementText: Enzymes lower activation energy but not the energy released
mcqs.explain: Energy is required to break bonds within the substrate, and the enzyme reduces this activation energy. The energy yield when bonds form in the products is a property of the reaction and is not changed.
rationales: A student who reads the lower catalysed curve as lower energy throughout picks this. In fact only the peak is lowered; substrate and products are at the same levels with or without the enzyme.

Energy is required to break bonds within the substrate, and the enzyme reduces this activation energy. The energy yield when bonds form in the products is a property of the reaction and is not changed.
A student who thinks the enzyme is an energy source picks this. In fact the enzyme supplies no energy; it lowers the barrier so that more substrate molecules already have enough energy to react.
A student who thinks bond breaking releases energy picks this. In fact energy is required to break bonds; energy is released when the bonds of the products are made.

mcqs.q: In an energy diagram for a reaction, the substrate is at 40 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products are at 15 kJ mol⁻¹. The highest energy reached during the reaction is 90 kJ mol⁻¹ without an enzyme and 60 kJ mol⁻¹ with the enzyme. For the enzyme-catalysed reaction, what are the activation energy and the overall energy yield?
options: activation energy 60 kJ mol⁻¹; energy yield 25 kJ mol⁻¹
activation energy 20 kJ mol⁻¹; energy yield 45 kJ mol⁻¹
activation energy 20 kJ mol⁻¹; energy yield 25 kJ mol⁻¹
activation energy 50 kJ mol⁻¹; energy yield 25 kJ mol⁻¹
mcqs.specStatementText: Enzymes lower activation energy but not the energy released
mcqs.explain: Activation energy is the rise from substrate to the highest point: 60 − 40 = 20 kJ mol⁻¹ with the enzyme. The energy yield is substrate minus products: 40 − 15 = 25 kJ mol⁻¹, the same as without the enzyme.
rationales: A student who reads the peak's value from the axis as the activation energy picks this. Activation energy is measured from the substrate level, so it is 60 − 40 = 20 kJ mol⁻¹.

A student who reads the energy released as the fall from the peak to the products (60 − 15) picks this. That fall includes the activation energy that was put in; the yield is substrate minus products, 25 kJ mol⁻¹.

Activation energy is the rise from substrate to the highest point: 60 − 40 = 20 kJ mol⁻¹ with the enzyme. The energy yield is substrate minus products: 40 − 15 = 25 kJ mol⁻¹, the same as without the enzyme.

A student who thinks the enzyme supplies energy rather than lowering the barrier keeps the uncatalysed value, 90 − 40 = 50 kJ mol⁻¹. With the enzyme the highest point is 60 kJ mol⁻¹, so the activation energy is 20 kJ mol⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Which statement about intracellular and extracellular enzyme-catalysed reactions is correct?
options: Digestion in the gut is intracellular, because food is broken down inside the cells that line it.
The Krebs cycle is extracellular, because it breaks down food in the gut to release its energy.
Extracellular enzymes such as pepsin are made outside cells, which is why they act outside them.
Glycolysis is intracellular; chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular.
mcqs.specStatementText: Enzymes act inside cells or are secreted to act outside
mcqs.explain: Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle take place inside cells and are intracellular. Digestive enzymes are secreted into the gut lumen and act outside cells, so chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular.
rationales: A student who merges absorption with digestion picks this. In fact digestive enzymes are secreted and act in the gut lumen, outside cells; only the products are absorbed.
A student who conflates respiration with digestion picks this. In fact the Krebs cycle occurs inside cells, in mitochondria, and its substrates are products of digestion that cells have absorbed.
A student who reads 'extracellular' as describing where the enzyme is made picks this. In fact all enzymes are synthesized inside cells; extracellular enzymes are secreted to act outside.

Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle take place inside cells and are intracellular. Digestive enzymes are secreted into the gut lumen and act outside cells, so chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular.

mcqs.q: A resting mammal produces heat continuously, even when it is not shivering and its muscles are relaxed. Why is this heat production inevitable?
options: No metabolic reaction transfers energy with 100% efficiency, so part of the energy of every reaction becomes heat.
Heat is produced only by dedicated reactions, such as those in shivering muscle, which are switched on when cold.
Breaking the bonds in glucose releases energy directly as heat before any of it is transferred to make ATP.
Only mammals and birds produce metabolic heat, because in other animals energy transfer has no losses.
mcqs.specStatementText: Metabolism always makes heat, and some animals depend on it
mcqs.explain: Heat generation is inevitable because metabolic reactions are not 100% efficient in energy transfer. Every reaction in every cell releases some heat, and mammals and birds depend on this to maintain a constant body temperature.
rationales: Heat generation is inevitable because metabolic reactions are not 100% efficient in energy transfer. Every reaction in every cell releases some heat, and mammals and birds depend on this to maintain a constant body temperature.
A student who thinks heat comes only from special mechanisms picks this, but the stem says the animal is not shivering. In fact all metabolic reactions release some heat as an unavoidable by-product.
A student who thinks bond breaking releases energy picks this. In fact breaking bonds requires energy; heat arises because the energy released as new bonds form is not all captured in ATP.

A student who takes 'warm-blooded' to mean 'heat-producing' picks this. In fact every organism's metabolism releases heat; mammals and birds are distinctive in relying on it for a constant body temperature.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes the Calvin cycle and the Krebs cycle from glycolysis?
options: The cycles regenerate all of their intermediates and so produce no net product, whereas glycolysis produces pyruvate as its end product.
In the cycles an intermediate used in the first step is regenerated in the last, whereas glycolysis runs from glucose to pyruvate in a chain.
The cycles use up their starting compound on every turn, so it must be supplied continuously from outside, unlike the glucose used in glycolysis.
The cycles take place in the gut, where food is broken down to release its energy, whereas glycolysis takes place inside cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pathways run as a line or as a cycle
mcqs.explain: A cyclical pathway regenerates one intermediate with each turn: RuBP in the Calvin cycle and oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle. Glycolysis is linear, converting glucose through a series of intermediates to pyruvate with nothing regenerated.
rationales: A student who thinks a cycle makes nothing new picks this. In fact substrates enter and products leave each cycle: the Krebs cycle releases carbon dioxide and reduced NAD, and the Calvin cycle releases triose phosphate.

A cyclical pathway regenerates one intermediate with each turn: RuBP in the Calvin cycle and oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle. Glycolysis is linear, converting glucose through a series of intermediates to pyruvate with nothing regenerated.
A student who applies linear-pathway logic to cycles picks this. In fact the starting compound of a cycle is what is regenerated; it is glycolysis whose starting substrate, glucose, is consumed.
A student who conflates the Krebs cycle with digestion picks this. In fact both cycles are intracellular: the Krebs cycle in mitochondria and the Calvin cycle in chloroplasts.

mcqs.q: Which statement about non-competitive inhibition at an allosteric site is correct?
options: The inhibitor binds permanently to the allosteric site, so the enzyme is inactivated for the rest of its life.
Any molecule of a suitable size can occupy the allosteric site, and it denatures the enzyme when it does so.
The inhibitor binds reversibly away from the active site, and the resulting shape change stops catalysis.
The inhibitor occupies the active site, and adding more substrate displaces it and restores the rate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Binding at an allosteric site reshapes the active site
mcqs.explain: Only specific substances bind to an allosteric site. Binding causes interactions within the enzyme that lead to conformational changes, altering the active site enough to prevent catalysis; the binding is reversible.
rationales: A student who reads 'non-competitive' as 'irreversible' picks this. In fact binding at an allosteric site is reversible; the enzyme regains activity when the inhibitor leaves.
A student who equates inhibition with denaturation picks this. In fact only specific substances bind to an allosteric site, and the conformational change is reversible, not denaturation.

Only specific substances bind to an allosteric site. Binding causes interactions within the enzyme that lead to conformational changes, altering the active site enough to prevent catalysis; the binding is reversible.

A student who applies the competitive mechanism to all inhibitors picks this. In fact a non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere, so extra substrate cannot displace it and the maximum rate stays lowered.

mcqs.q: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction was measured at six increasing substrate concentrations, without and with inhibitor X. Without X the rates were 20, 35, 50, 58, 60 and 60 units. With X they were 8, 18, 33, 48, 57 and 60 units. What type of inhibitor is X?
options: Non-competitive, because X lowers the rate at most concentrations, which shows that it is bound irreversibly.
Non-competitive, because a competitive inhibitor would have kept the rate low at every substrate concentration.
Either type, because raising the substrate concentration overcomes both competitive and non-competitive inhibitors.
Competitive, because at high substrate concentration the inhibited rate reaches the uninhibited maximum.
mcqs.specStatementText: Competitive inhibitors share the active site with the substrate
mcqs.explain: With X the rate is lower at low substrate concentration but climbs to the same maximum of 60 units. Substrate outcompetes the inhibitor for the active site at high concentration, the defining feature of competitive inhibition.
rationales: A student who thinks non-competitive means irreversible picks this. In fact an irreversible or non-competitive inhibitor would lower the maximum rate; here the maximum is fully recovered.

A student who thinks a competitive inhibitor permanently blocks the active site picks this. In fact competitive inhibition is reversible and is overcome by high substrate concentration, as the data show.

A student who thinks extra substrate defeats any inhibitor picks this. In fact substrate cannot displace a non-competitive inhibitor from an allosteric site, so recovery of the maximum rate identifies X as competitive.

With X the rate is lower at low substrate concentration but climbs to the same maximum of 60 units. Substrate outcompetes the inhibitor for the active site at high concentration, the defining feature of competitive inhibition.

mcqs.q: Statins are drugs prescribed to reduce blood cholesterol. How do they act?
options: They resemble the substrate of an enzyme in the cholesterol synthesis pathway and bind reversibly to its active site.
They hydrolyse cholesterol molecules that are already circulating in the blood into products that are excreted.
They bind permanently to the active site of the enzyme, so cholesterol synthesis stops for the rest of life.
They denature the cholesterol-synthesizing enzyme so that it can no longer fold into its working shape.
mcqs.specStatementText: Competitive inhibitors share the active site with the substrate
mcqs.explain: Statins are competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme in the pathway that synthesizes cholesterol. Because they resemble the substrate they compete for the active site, reducing the rate of cholesterol production.
rationales: Statins are competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme in the pathway that synthesizes cholesterol. Because they resemble the substrate they compete for the active site, reducing the rate of cholesterol production.
A student who assumes 'lowering cholesterol' means removing it picks this. In fact statins are enzyme inhibitors that reduce cholesterol synthesis; they do not break cholesterol down.
A student who thinks a competitive inhibitor blocks the site for good picks this. In fact binding is reversible, which is why statins must be taken continuously to keep cholesterol low.
A student who equates inhibition with denaturation picks this. In fact statins bind reversibly to an intact enzyme's active site; the enzyme is unchanged when the statin leaves.

mcqs.q: In bacteria, threonine is converted into isoleucine by a pathway of five enzyme-catalysed steps. What happens when isoleucine is added to a growing culture?
options: Isoleucine binds to the enzyme of the final step, the one that produced it, and blocks that single step only.
Isoleucine binds to an allosteric site on the first enzyme, reversibly reducing the pathway's activity.
The five enzymes are broken down, so the pathway cannot restart after the isoleucine is used up.
Isoleucine competes with threonine for the active site of the first enzyme, blocking it competitively.
mcqs.specStatementText: The end product switches off the first enzyme
mcqs.explain: This is feedback inhibition: the end product, isoleucine, binds to an allosteric site on threonine deaminase, the first enzyme of the pathway. Binding is reversible, so the pathway resumes when isoleucine is used up.
rationales: A student who reasons from proximity on the diagram picks this. In fact the end product inhibits the first enzyme, which stops the whole pathway and prevents intermediates from accumulating.

This is feedback inhibition: the end product, isoleucine, binds to an allosteric site on threonine deaminase, the first enzyme of the pathway. Binding is reversible, so the pathway resumes when isoleucine is used up.
A student who thinks feedback inhibition is permanent picks this. In fact the enzymes are unchanged; inhibition is released as soon as the isoleucine concentration falls.
A student who defaults to the active site for any inhibitor picks this. In fact isoleucine does not resemble threonine closely enough to compete; it binds to a separate allosteric site.

mcqs.q: Penicillin inhibits transpeptidases, the bacterial enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan in the cell wall. Which statement correctly describes both the action of penicillin and how bacteria become resistant to it?
options: Penicillin competes reversibly with the substrate for the active site; bacteria resist it by producing extra substrate that outcompetes the drug molecules.
Penicillin binds to an allosteric site on transpeptidase and inactivates it permanently; resistant bacteria have a transpeptidase that lacks the allosteric site.
Penicillin bonds irreversibly to the active site, changing it chemically; a changed transpeptidase that penicillin cannot bind confers resistance.
Bacteria exposed to penicillin alter their own transpeptidase during their lifetime and pass this acquired change to their offspring.
mcqs.specStatementText: Some inhibitors change the active site for good
mcqs.explain: Mechanism-based inhibition is a consequence of chemical changes to the active site caused by the irreversible binding of an inhibitor. Resistance is conferred by a mutant transpeptidase whose altered active site still cross-links peptidoglycan but does not bind penicillin.
rationales: A student who assumes every active-site inhibitor is competitive picks this. In fact penicillin binds covalently and irreversibly, so extra substrate cannot displace it; resistance requires a changed enzyme.

A student who assumes that any irreversible inhibitor must be acting non-competitively at an allosteric site picks this. In fact penicillin binds at the active site and changes it chemically; resistance comes from an altered active site that still cross-links peptidoglycan but no longer binds penicillin.

Mechanism-based inhibition is a consequence of chemical changes to the active site caused by the irreversible binding of an inhibitor. Resistance is conferred by a mutant transpeptidase whose altered active site still cross-links peptidoglycan but does not bind penicillin.
A student who thinks exposure causes the change picks this. In fact the altered transpeptidase arises by mutation; penicillin selects the bacteria that already carry it, and they pass it on.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic C1.1 Enzymes and metabolism
